info.bio: Truly was a band formed in the wake of the grunge era, featuring, former Soundgarden bassist Hiro Yamamoto, one-time Screaming Trees drummer Mark Pickerel and singer Robert Roth. They released two full-length studio albums: "Fast Stories... from Kid Coma" in 1995 and "Feeling You Up" in 1998. They were notable for their dense, bass-heavy sound, despite only being a three-piece, recalling Black Sabbath and Yamamoto's previous band. Despite a fair amount of critical acclaim, they had limited commercial success.

scenes.desc: El grunge, revival del hard rock de los setenta y renacimiento musical de Seattle, fue uno de los grandes fenómenos de los noventa (casi solo en EE UU). Green River lo inauguran (Come On Down) y Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, Melvins y Mudhoney fijan sus cuatro puntos cardinales; Nirvana, con Nevermind, lo convierten en una tragaperras y en la banda sonora de la crisis nerviosa de una generación. Después, Alice In Chains (Dirt), Foo Fighters, Hammerbox, GodHeadSilo, Everclear, Stone Temple Pilots, Tool (el grupo más innovador de la segunda generación: Aenima, Lateralus), God Machine, Helmet, Quicksand, Urge Overkill, los Smashing Pumpkins (Siamese Dream, Mellon Collie), Scarce, Creed, Bush, Manic Street Preachers, Silverchair.

podcast.title: Post-Soundgarden Project – Featuring Screaming Trees Members
podcast.body: After leaving Soundgarden in 1989 to complete his master's degree, Hiro Yamamoto played in a band called Truly. This group also featured a couple of members from Screaming Trees, another band that had recorded at Jack Endino's Reciprocal Recording studio. "Between classes, he'd played in a band called Truly, which featured a couple of members of the screaming trees."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Crisis of Faith and Music Hiatus (1957)
xref.body: Little Richard, one of the first rock and roll stars and one of the first black rock and roll stars, experienced a crisis of faith in 1957 while in the middle of a tour of Australia. This crisis was triggered by dreaming of his own damnation, which he attributed largely to his closeted gayness. He subsequently quit the music business for five years, and after returning, he never truly regained the level of success and prominence he had enjoyed in the mid-1950s. "dreaming of his own damn nation, much of which had to do with his closeted gainess."

xref.title: Ringo Starr's Worry Over Montreal Threats (1964)
xref.body: Ringo Starr expressed genuine worry about the death threats received during The Beatles' 1964 Montreal concerts. He recalled that some individuals targeted him "as an English Jew," despite him not being Jewish, noting that while threats were often taken "in stride," this particular incident, despite more police presence, was one of the few times he was truly concerned. "Some people decided to make an example of me as an English Jew. The one major fault is, I'm not Jewish. Threats we took in stride. I mean, suddenly there'd be a few more cops, but this was one of the few times I was really worried."

xref.title: Production of "I Feel Love" (1977)
xref.body: Giorgio Moroder produced Donna Summer's 1977 track "I Feel Love," which became known as the first truly computerized and synthesized dance single. His work on this track incorporated elements that later influenced artists like Daniel Miller of The Normal. "That was the first truly computerized, slashed synthesized dance single, which she created with the help of producer George Eomeroder."

xref.title: Hiro Yamamoto's Departure (1989) – Pursuit of Education
xref.body: In 1989, bassist Hiro Yamamoto left Soundgarden to finish his master's degree in physical chemistry. After leaving the band, he continued his musical pursuits by playing in a band called Truly, which included members of Screaming Trees. "In 1989, there was a lineup change when bass player Hero Yamamoto quit to finish his master's degree in physical chemistry."

xref.title: Hospital Reunion (2008)
xref.body: Following Travis Barker's severe injuries from the plane crash, Mark Hoppus was among the first to visit him in the hospital, and Tom Delonge also made the trip. The three members of Blink-182 met in a "sobering reunion" at Travis's bedside, prompting a realization for all three about what truly mattered in their lives and relationships. "The three guys met up in the hospital in a pretty sobering reunion."

xref.title: Autobiographical Reflection
xref.body: In his autobiography, Travis Barker reflects on how life-altering events, such as his near-fatal plane crash, clarify one's understanding of personal relationships. He articulates a realization about who truly matters in life. "He writes in his autobiography that comes to point in life when you realize who really matters, who never did, and who always will."

xref.title: Breakthrough Delay
xref.body: The band's career did not truly begin to flourish until the release of their fourth album, highlighting that not all bands achieve immediate widespread success. "Their career really didn't start to blossom until their fourth album."

xref.title: Denial of Goth Affiliation
xref.body: Robert Smith later disavowed The Cure's Goth label, claiming it was a "big misunderstanding" and that they were never truly a Goth band. "And Robert Smith would later claim that the cure were never really Goth in the first place."

xref.title: Goth Influence and Success
xref.body: Depeche Mode, though not originally or truly a Goth band, became influenced by Goth music as the 1980s progressed, leading to significant record sales and, for many new fans, a path back to Goth itself. "as the 1980s wore on, they were influenced by this music and ended up selling a gazillion records as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Major Label Punk
xref.body: The Ramones were cited as an example of a punk band that was signed to a major label. Their presence on a major label was used to argue that "subverting the system from within" could be a truly punk and alternative approach. "And weren't the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and the Clash all in major labels?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Need for Opportunity
xref.body: Despite good reviews and industry recognition, Kid Rock needed a specific "window of opportunity" where rock and rap "synced up just so" for his career to truly take off. "All he needed was a window of opportunity. That moment when Rock and Rap synced up just so."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Online Availability of Sheep Material
xref.body: Although *Sheep* is not part of Nirvana's official discography, much of its material is not truly lost due to its availability on the internet. "That record isn't part of the band's official discography, but thanks to the magic of the internet, it isn't exactly lost."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Kurt Cobain Legacy
xref.body: After Kurt Cobain's death, fans wondered what material he had left behind. The *With the Lights Out* box set, released over 10 years later, addressed this by compiling remaining material, but it was noted that "the real answer was not much" in terms of truly finished works. "And Kurt died, fans wondered what he had left behind. Had to be something, right? Well, the real answer was not much."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Mortem Influence Celebration
xref.body: Charles Mingus was revered by his fellow jazz artists during his lifetime, but it was only after he passed away in 1979 that his profound influence on jazz was truly celebrated. "It was only after he passed away in 1979 that his influence on jazz was truly celebrated."

xref.title: Profound Memory Loss and Identity Crisis
xref.body: After being discharged from the hospital following his meningitis battle, Johnny Lydon suffered from severe memory loss that persisted for about four years, leaving him unable to recall his own name, his parents' names, or virtually anything from his past. He later reflected that this ordeal forced him to completely rebuild his identity, calling the meningitis "God's greatest gift" because it compelled him to discover who he truly was. "He couldn't remember his name or the name of his mom and dad."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Prominence in Early 80s Rockabilly
xref.body: The Stray Cats were a prominent band in the "alt-rock style rockabilly" genre, which was very big in the early 1980s for about 18 months. However, this style subsequently faded out and has never truly had a full-blown revival in the alt-rock sense. "It was really big in the very early 80s with bands like the Stray Cats, but then it just kind of went away."

xref.body: Dave Grohl has garnered a widespread reputation and is described as truly deserving the title of "the nicest man in rock," based on observed interactions and his overall demeanor. "Dave really does deserve the title as the nicest man in rock."

xref.title: Shoegaze Influence
xref.body: Silver Sun Pickups were noted as a later band whose music demonstrates the continuing influence of Shoegaze, a genre that retreated into the background after the rise of Grunge but never truly disappeared. "Its influences can still be felt today and later bands like Silver Sun pickups."

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Pogo Invention
xref.body: Sid Vicious, who later became the bassist for the Sex Pistols, is credited in legend as the inventor of the Pogo dance. He reportedly started pogoing to mock non-punks who attended the band's shows, as he felt they didn't truly belong. Another account from Shane McGowan suggests Sid's tight leather poncho restricted his dance movements to just jumping. "legend says he started Pogoing as a way of mocking non-punks who came to see the pistols."

xref.title: Theories Behind Unreleased Album
xref.body: Two main theories exist regarding the unreleased Ian McCulloch/Johnny Marr album. One suggests the theft story was fabricated by Ian to facilitate his return to Echo and the Bunnyman without interference from the collaboration. Another theory proposes the music was of poor quality due to frequent arguments between Ian and Johnny, indicating the album might never have been truly completed. "The theory is that Ian and Johnny made up the story because Ian wanted to get back with the Bunnieman, and this project would have ruined everything. Another theory is that the music was crap because Ian and Johnny were arguing so much that an album never really was completed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Theories Behind Unreleased Album
xref.body: The unreleased collaboration album between Johnny Marr and Ian McCulloch is surrounded by speculation. One theory posits that the theft story was concocted to allow Ian McCulloch to rejoin Echo and the Bunnyman without complications. Another suggests the album was never truly completed due to creative conflicts and poor quality resulting from frequent arguments between Marr and McCulloch. "The theory is that Ian and Johnny made up the story because Ian wanted to get back with the Bunnieman, and this project would have ruined everything. Another theory is that the music was crap because Ian and Johnny were arguing so much that an album never really was completed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Zach de la Rocha's Fan Engagement and Disillusionment
xref.body: Zach de la Rocha often cultivated strong relationships with fans by holding political discussions in venue parking lots after shows with groups of kids. However, he felt disillusioned when only a small fraction (e.g., 15 kids out of a 5,000-person crowd) stayed, questioning if their political message was truly getting through or if fans were merely pretending to engage. "For example, it was an uncommon to find Zach D. Leroka in the parking lot of the venue after the show holding a political discussion with 15 kids."
